title: Making an incremental RPG solo: from hand-written scripts with a chatbot to an AI assistant inside the project
author: Annual_River_6559
selftext:
Hey! I'm making Spheromancer, an incremental clicker with RPG elements in a fantasy setting. You fight Spheres with different elemental weaknesses, collect and evolve minions into a squad, learn skills and spells, craft gear, hunt Spheres to lock them in your Prison for passive income, and go on raids for loot.

I started development at the beginning of this year. I'd never made a game before and had never even opened Unity. I just started designing the game, figuring out the engine, watching YouTube tutorials and trying out assets to piece together the technical base: database, inventory, damage, elements, UI switching and so on. I knew people were already using AI in development, but I had no idea how exactly or what it could actually do.

**Art.** The first thing I used AI for was images: enemies, icons, UI parts, backgrounds. Mostly Nano Banana. Some of the images I reworked in Photoshop.

**Code through a chatbot.** Then I found out Google's chat could help with small scripts. For a long time I built the game's systems like this: ask a question, paste the current script, get a guess about how to do something or why it doesn't work. Most of the time nothing worked, of course, haha. But I still managed to build most of the game and get it, with bugs and rough edges, to the first release. Everything in Unity I did by hand: scene setup, rewriting scripts, architecture. That "outdated" approach was definitely useful for learning. Whether it still makes sense today is another question.

**First release and switching to an AI assistant.** After launching on itch I got a round of feedback and \~1500 browser plays. There were lots of bugs I couldn't find and fix on my own before release. Friends suggested trying a modern model like Claude to check the game. That's how I found out my workflow was "a bit" outdated: an AI assistant can connect straight to the project folder, see the whole context and work "almost without mistakes". It sped things up a lot and changed how I work on the game.

Honestly, that made me happy rather than upset, because when I started I wanted to do game design, not programming. Design and planning are still on the creator though. You need to clearly describe the result you want and think through a system or feature first, and only then work with the AI. Still, it's impressive how smart these models have become, how well they understand tasks and write code. For people who've been in the industry for years it must be mind-blowing.

**Bottom line.** So that's my path on this project: from writing scripts almost by hand to a modern workflow. I get that all of this could've been done waaay faster with a good coding AI from the start, without digging through everything manually. But that's how it went for me.



Game on Itch (web / windows): [https://lexiany13.itch.io/spheromancer](https://lexiany13.itch.io/spheromancer)
